newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl reaffirms need for strict EMU entry criteria.
newsitem.headline: Kohl reaffirms need for strict EMU entry criteria.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, reaffirming his government's stand on European Monetary Union (EMU) on Sunday, said the project should start on schedule in January 1999 and strictly follow rules outlined in the Maastricht Treaty.

"The Chancellor insisted that both the stability criteria laid down by the Maastricht Treaty and the timetable have to be adhered to," said a government summary of remarks from a speech Kohl was due to give in Frankfurt at a trade fair.
"Securing Germany's future also means continuing the work of European integration with the completion of monetary and economic union," the summary quoted him as saying.

Kohl also said the recent squabble with the Bundesbank over Bonn's plans to revalue the bank's gold and currency reserves was no attack on the central bank's independence and that the reserves need to be revalued before the euro's start.
"He stated clearly and categorically that the revalution in no way constituted an infringement of the Bundesbank's independence," the statement said.

"Between the government and the Bundesbank there was full agreement that with transition to the euro, the Bundesbank's reserves, which were currently valued at a very low level, should be progressively revalued at a higher level," it said.
The statement also said that Kohl was committed to further cooperation between Bonn and the Bundesbank.

Bonn has been forced to seek additional funds after it lost a public battle with the Bundesbank over its intention to revalue central bank reserves and use the booked profits to help cut debt and deficit levels to meet Maastricht criteria.
A Bundesbank council member, Franz-Christoph Zeitler, said on Saturday the central bank and Bonn were close to a compromise on Bonn's plans to revalue the reserves.

One solution envisaged by economists is for revaluation proceeds to be transferred to Bonn beginning in 1998 or 1999 to help reduce debt and not in 1997, the year when Germany's finances will be judged for entry into currency union.

Kohl's comments came as Finance Minister Theo Waigel told German television on Sunday he wants to radically cut spending and push through the privatisation of more government assets to help Bonn balance its books in 1998.
Waigel also said he was sure savings at both federal and state level this year would mean Germany would meet the entry criteria needed to qualify for Europe's single currency.

Germany is viewed by many independent economists as needing to take dramatic action to cut its budget deficit to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), a level Waigel said must be met by nations seeking to enter currency union.
